proposedTopics.title: Linked List
proposedTopics.description: Pointer-based sequential structure. Reuses the fast/slow pointer idea from Two Pointers in a context with no random access.

proposedTopics.title: Reversal
proposedTopics.description: Walk the list rewiring each node's next pointer to the previous node, tracking prev/curr/next explicitly (or via recursion). Recognize: "reverse the list" or a sublist of it.

proposedTopics.title: Fast & slow pointers (list)
proposedTopics.description: Two pointers advancing at different speeds through a list find cycles, midpoints, or the kth-from-end node without a second pass. Recognize: cycle detection, "find the middle", palindrome check without extra storage.

proposedTopics.title: Merge / merge-k-lists
proposedTopics.description: Repeatedly take the smaller head across lists (pairwise merge, or a heap for k lists) to build one sorted list. Recognize: "merge sorted lists", building block for merge sort on lists.

proposedTopics.title: Dummy-node manipulation
proposedTopics.description: A dummy head node before the real head removes edge cases when the operation might affect the head itself. Recognize: "remove/insert near the head", list partitioning.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for in-place pointer reversal on a linked list? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: "reverse the list" (or a sublist / every k nodes), reordering that needs next-pointers flipped rather than values copied. Pitfall: overwriting curr.next before you've saved it — capture next = curr.next FIRST each iteration, or you lose the rest of the list. Related: Swap Nodes in Pairs is reversal with k=2; Reverse Nodes in k-Group tiles this per block.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the iterative list-reversal kernel in your language of choice: given a head, return the head of the reversed list using three pointers.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: prev = null, curr = head; each step: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. Loop until curr is null; return prev. Invariant: everything from prev backward is already reversed, everything from curr forward is untouched.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Linked List (Easy) — reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Three-pointer prev/curr/next sweep, flipping each next pointer as you go; prev is the answer.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Linked List II (Medium) — reverse the sublist from position left to right (1-indexed) in one pass.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dummy head, walk to the node before left, then reverse exactly (right-left) links by repeatedly splicing the next node to the front of the reversed segment.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Reverse Nodes in k-Group (Hard) — reverse the list in consecutive groups of k, leaving a trailing remainder of fewer than k nodes as-is.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: First count/check that k nodes remain, reverse that block, then recurse (or iterate) linking the reversed block's tail to the next block's result.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for fast & slow pointers on a linked list? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: detect a cycle, find the middle, find the kth-from-end, or check a palindrome without extra storage. Pitfall: dereferencing fast/fast.next without null-guarding both (odd vs even length) — the loop condition must be `fast && fast.next`. Related: Palindrome Linked List finds the midpoint then reverses the second half.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write Floyd's cycle-detection kernel in your language of choice: given a head, return whether the list has a cycle, and adapt it to also return the midpoint node.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: slow = head, fast = head; each step slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they meet there's a cycle. When fast reaches the end (no cycle), slow sits on the middle. Guard the loop with `fast && fast.next`.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Linked List Cycle (Easy) — return true if the linked list contains a cycle.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Advance slow by 1 and fast by 2; a cycle exists iff they ever point at the same node.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Middle of the Linked List (Easy) — return the middle node (the second middle if the length is even).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: When fast walks two steps per slow step, slow lands on the middle as fast falls off the end.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Linked List Cycle II (Medium) — return the node where the cycle begins, or null if there is none.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: After slow and fast meet inside the cycle, reset one pointer to head and advance both by 1 — they meet at the cycle's entry (Floyd's second phase).

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for the pairwise sorted-merge pattern on lists? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: "merge sorted lists", or a divide-and-conquer that needs a merge step (merge sort on a list). Pitfall: forgetting to attach the non-empty remainder after one list runs out, or not using a dummy head so you fumble the first node. Related: Merge k Sorted Lists (carded under Heap / Priority Queue) generalizes this to k-way via a heap.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the two-list sorted-merge kernel in your language of choice: given two sorted heads, splice them into one sorted list.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dummy head, tail pointer; while both non-null append the smaller head and advance that list; finally attach whichever remainder is left. Invariant: everything from dummy to tail is sorted and already placed.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Merge Two Sorted Lists (Easy) — splice two sorted lists into one sorted list.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dummy head + tail; repeatedly link the smaller of the two current heads, then attach the leftover tail.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Sort List (Medium) — sort a linked list in O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Merge sort on the list: fast/slow to split at the midpoint, recurse on each half, then reuse the two-list merge to combine.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for a dummy head node? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: an insert/delete that might change the head itself, list partitioning, or building a new list from scratch. Pitfall: returning the original head instead of dummy.next (the real head may have been removed), or a two-pointer gap set to n instead of n+1 off-by-one. Related: Partition List builds two dummy-headed sublists; Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II deletes runs behind a dummy.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the remove-nth-from-end kernel in your language of choice: given a head and n, delete the nth node from the end in one pass using a dummy head and a gap.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Dummy before head; advance a lead pointer n+1 steps, then move lead and a trail pointer together until lead is null — trail now sits just before the target, so set trail.next = trail.next.next. Return dummy.next.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Remove Nth Node From End of List (Medium) — remove the nth node from the end and return the head.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Two pointers with an n+1 gap behind a dummy head; when the lead falls off the end the trailing pointer is right before the node to unlink.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Add Two Numbers (Medium) — two numbers stored as digit lists in reverse order; return their sum as a list.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Walk both lists behind a dummy head, summing digit + carry each step; keep going while either list or the carry is non-zero.
